query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation in multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature is driven by cyclic mechanical removal of protective oxide films, which exposes phase boundaries with differing electrochemical potentials that act as micro-galvanic cells, thereby enhancing localized corrosion and overall material loss.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with intrinsic phase partitioning in its as-fabricated state, exhibiting established protective oxide layers under static conditions.
generation.intervention: Perform an elevated-temperature tribocorrosion experiment where one sample is subjected to both mechanical wear (via sliding under controlled load) and a corrosive chloride-containing environment, while a matched control is exposed to the corrosive environment alone without mechanical contact.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (600–700°C), constant mechanical load during sliding, and a fixed corrosive medium composition (e.g., chloride-containing solution) to ensure realistic service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The periodic removal of the protective oxide film at phase boundaries leads to direct exposure of chemically dissimilar phases, establishing micro-galvanic cells that accelerate localized corrosion.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear cyclically disrupts the naturally forming protective oxide layer. At elevated temperatures, the increased kinetics of oxidation and corrosion cause the exposed phase boundaries—each with different electrochemical potentials—to develop micro-galvanic couplings. These couplings accelerate the dissolution of the more reactive phases, thereby increasing the overall degradation beyond the simple sum of wear and corrosion acting independently.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the corrosion-only control, the sample undergoing simultaneous wear and corrosion will exhibit significantly higher total degradation. Wear damage will be exacerbated by the inability of the oxide film to reform consistently, and corrosion will be enhanced at the phase boundaries, resulting in a synergistic increase in both wear volume and corrosion current.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the same alloy sample undergoing only the corrosive environment at elevated temperature without mechanical wear.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to eutectic high-entropy alloys with inherent phase heterogeneity under high-temperature, chloride-containing conditions, where the formation and removal dynamics of oxide films are critical. It assumes no additional passivating agents are present that could otherwise stabilize the oxide layer.
generation.uncertainty: While the hypothesis is supported by observations of oxide film rupture and micro-galvanic corrosion in similar systems, quantitative contributions of wear vs. corrosion under these dynamic conditions remain uncertain and require in situ analysis for precise determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in situ high-temperature tribocorrosion tests using scanning electron microscopy coupled with on-line electrochemical potential measurements. Compare a test sample (subjected to both sliding wear and a corrosive chloride-containing environment) against a control sample exposed only to corrosion under the same temperature and environmental conditions. Monitor oxide film formation and removal cycles, microstructural changes at phase boundaries, friction coefficients, wear volumes, and electrochemical signatures (such as transient potential fluctuations) during the tests.
measurements: Real-time imaging of the oxide film on the worn surface
Electrochemical impedance and polarization curves to capture corrosion kinetics
Wear volume measurement and friction coefficient data
Surface chemical analysis to detect local corrosion at phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the test sample does not exhibit a statistically significant correlation between mechanical oxide film disruption and enhanced localized corrosion (i.e., if degradation in the coupled wear-corrosion test is not greater than the sum of individual wear and corrosion effects or if no distinct micro-galvanic attack is observed at phase boundaries), then the hypothesis that cyclic mechanical oxide removal drives accelerated degradation via micro-galvanic coupling would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

AbstractIn this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5.Keywords: high-entropy alloy (HEA), compositionally complex alloy (CCA), spark plasma sinterin

In this work, the influence of temperature on the corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution was investigated using electrochemical measurement, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Results show that the passive film of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is stable in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at low temperatures, while an unstable film forms on the alloy at high temperatures. Furthermore, temperature changes the proportion of hydroxide and oxide in Fe and Cr, but it has no noticeable effect on Al and Ni, which is a significant factor on the passive behavior. L12 phase exhibits good corrosion resistance at different temperatures. Pitting occurred on B2 phase in the chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution at a low temperature of 5 °C, while pitting and dissolution take place on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in the acid solution at room temperature and above.

Overall, ip raises, transpassive potential (Eb) falls, and the passive range becomes narrower with an increase in environmental temperature, indicating that it is more difficult to passivate the alloy, and the passive film is subject to break at high temperature. The results confirmed that an increase in temperature promotes the dissolution of the EHEAs in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution containing Cl−. In addition, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 does not possess satisfactory pitting resistance at relatively high environmental temperatures. The Nyquist plot of the EHEA at a temperature of 5 °C exhibits a capacitive loop and an inductive loop at high and low frequencies, respectively. decision.trend: Early work on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and related eutectic high-entropy alloys established their high strength and ductility at elevated temperature (PMC4145285). Subsequent studies explored high-temperature wear in multi-phase AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5, showing that complex microstructures with protective oxides can enhance wear resistance (PMC7515071). More recent investigations of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in chloride-containing acid solutions at different temperatures revealed corrosion susceptibility driven by phase-specific reactivity and passive-film stability (PMC9319277). However, none directly addressed the combined effects of wear and corrosion in a single elevated-temperature test, leaving the mechanisms of their accelerated synergy poorly understood.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how periodic mechanical removal of protective oxides at high temperature and simultaneous electrochemical corrosion interact to amplify total degradation in these eutectic high-entropy alloys, nor how each phase contributes to the synergy under realistic service conditions.
decision.lever: Perform an elevated-temperature tribocorrosion experiment with on-line electrochemical potential measurements and simultaneous surface imaging (e.g., high-temperature in-situ scanning electron microscopy). Compare a wearing sample exposed to a corrosive environment against a matched control that experiences corrosion without mechanical contact to measure synergy. Key parameters: temperature (e.g., 600–700°C), normal load on the sliding contact, and corrosive medium composition (e.g., chloride content).
decision.why: Because earlier studies separately examined high-temperature wear (PMC7515071) and corrosion (PMC9319277) of eutectic HEAs, in-situ tribocorrosion testing will directly reveal the microstructural and dynamic changes caused by simultaneous mechanical and chemical attack, thereby distinguishing the hypothesized mechanism of oxide-film breakdown, micro-galvanic coupling at phase boundaries, and accelerated dissolution from simpler superpositions of wear and corrosion. A scientifically rigorous test is one that directly measures friction, wear volume, and electrochemical parameters in real-time while controlling temperature and environment, thus enabling clear differentiation of mechanical versus chemical contributions to overall degradation. The approach is falsified if increased damage does not correlate with repeated oxide removal or if no preferential phase attack or synergy effect is observed under these carefully matched conditions.
